military.label: Military history
military.date_label: Earlier roots · Howard 1961 · Keegan 1976 · multiple paradigms
military.description: Studies campaigns and combat alongside institutions, societies, maritime power, gender and remembrance. Ancient historians such as Thucydides and Polybius already wrote about testing reports of battle, terrain and military experience; they are precursors of the genre, not its founders. From about 1900 the field was practised in archive-based campaign and army histories, university lectureships and chairs (Oxford 1905 and 1909), official histories of the world wars and an American society (1933) and journal (1937; renamed Military Affairs in 1941); much of this work was written by or for officers. Howard’s contextual reconstruction, Keegan’s critical study of battle and debates over military revolutions supply different methods and explanations. Source access, narrative framing and geographic scope shape their claims.

military.scope_note: A research field with overlapping objects, not one school or a progression that supersedes campaign history. Delbrück, campaign and army historians, official historians and strategic writers supply distinct resources; military historians also reinterpret and criticize them. Keegan’s restricted battle definition leaves much colonial and guerrilla experience outside its frame. European military-revolution debates extend to overseas encounters without representing the whole world’s military historiography. Bourke, Winter and Nell retain distinct questions about bodies, mourning and recognition. Scholarly collaboration, library work, editing and archival limits are part of the field’s production. Ancient writers who narrated and judged wars (Thucydides, Polybius, Arrian) are selected precursors. The selected ancient passages document statements about testimony, terrain and experience. Separately checked modern passages discuss these authors; Kromayer explicitly engages Polybius’ criticism of Ephorus. These examples do not establish continuous transmission. Clausewitz ranked ancient military history the least useful while allowing instructive exceptions. Official and semi-official histories were written from privileged records, read in proof by participants or framed by sponsoring institutions; Liddell Hart criticised them in the period. Karsten (1984), describing the ‘new’ military history, concedes that ‘some scholars explored such questions in the past’. The selection before 1960 concentrates on British, American and German scholarship; other historiographies of war are not surveyed here.

strands.title: Campaign reconstruction and documentary limits
strands.focus: Howard, Tuchman and Wedgwood connect decisions and circumstances through different narrative practices. Source access and explanatory selection remain objects of criticism.
strands.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); The Guns of August (1962); The Thirty Years War (1938)

strands.title: Combat experience and critical testimony
strands.focus: Keegan joins questions about bodies and behavior to criticism of memoirs, rhetoric and physical possibility. His selected battle frame does not represent all forms of war.
strands.works: The Face of Battle (1976), available excerpt

strands.title: War studies, research and teaching
strands.focus: Howard became lecturer in military studies at King’s in 1953; a new War Studies programme was approved in 1955. His King’s work combines historical study with wider social, ethical and political inquiry. Earlier work and institutional support included Laughton’s naval history, Maurice’s chair of military studies (1927; the department closed in 1948), and C. K. Webster and Hancock, whose official-history work had drawn them to war as a field. Morgan-Owen and Finch (2022) call the story of Howard rescuing the subject from an academic wilderness one he ‘consciously cultivated’. Library access, publishing and translation collaboration form part of the research setting.
strands.works: The Franco-Prussian War (1961); War in European History (1976)

strands.title: Bodies, injury and masculinity

strands.works: Dismembering the Male (1996)

strands.title: Remembrance, mourning and recognition

strands.focus: Keegan’s later account and Bassford’s opposition distinguish cultural interpretation from the earlier reconstruction of combat. Political purpose and culture need not be mutually exclusive.
strands.works: A History of Warfare (1993), mediated; Bassford (1994)

strands.title: Recruitment as labor and household strategy
strands.focus: Lucassen and Zürcher compare state recruitment options with recruits’ and households’ responses. Pay and freedom vary independently; different systems coexist. Their explicit use of Tilly connects fiscal capacity to recruitment and resistance.
strands.works: “Conscription as Military Labour” (1998), 405–419

strands.title: Official and semi-official history and its critics
strands.focus: General-staff and cabinet historical sections wrote large histories of the world wars from privileged records. Edmonds’s British volumes (from 1922) were ‘based on the British official records’, written partly for ‘students at military schools’ and read in proof by officers who took part. Morison’s naval history was commissioned with full records access yet declared ‘in no sense an official history’ (1947). In the US Army’s series, Matloff and Snell, formerly instructors in history and English respectively and both wartime servicemen, joined the project in 1946; their volume’s foreword, by the Chief of Military History, asked readers to see its controversies as differences ‘among comrades in arms’ (1953), and its preface credits Helen McShane Bailey’s knowledge of the War Department’s records and Evelyn Cooper’s statistics. Liddell Hart attacked documentary and ‘camouflaged’ history (1930, 1944). During and after the Second World War official commissions drew academic historians to war (Hancock and Gowing from 1941, Webster and Frankland from 1950, Howard from 1959), under closure rules and secrecy. Later studies of the genre are unread here, and the German and French official histories are known only from period mentions.
strands.works: Edmonds, Military Operations, France and Belgium, 1914, vol. I (1922), preface; Liddell Hart, The Real War (1930), preface, and Why Don’t We Learn from History? (1944); Morison, Operations in North African Waters (1947), foreword and introduction; Matloff and Snell, Strategic Planning for Coalition Warfare, 1941–1942 (1953), foreword and preface; Hancock and Gowing, British War Economy (1949); Howard, Grand Strategy, vol. IV (1972)

strands.title: Campaign and army history as scholarship, c. 1898–1950
strands.focus: Oman’s art-of-war volume (1898) and Peninsular War (1902) worked from chronicles, Record Office papers and passages omitted from printed dispatches, treated veterans’ memoirs with caution and walked battlefields. Fortescue, a civilian, wrote the army’s history as political as well as military history (1899) and distrusted regimental histories; his 1914 definition held that ‘below a certain stage of civilisation, there can be no military history’, a boundary that bears on the field’s geographic scope. Parker’s preface (1928) proposes an institutional history of the Roman legions’ organisation, recruitment and service; the abbreviation list shows extensive inscription corpora, and the body is unread. Kromayer and Veith’s preface (1928) adds strategy and tactics to the antiquarian study of ancient armies and excludes the Orient, Carthage, Gauls and Germans. Howard (1961, as reported by Kitchen and Mitchell and by Strachan) later named regimental ‘nursery history’ and the historian’s duty to examine its ‘myth’.
strands.works: Oman, A History of the Art of War: The Middle Ages (1898) and A History of the Peninsular War, vol. I (1902), prefaces; Fortescue, A History of the British Army, vols. I–II (1899), preface, and Military History (1914); Parker, The Roman Legions (1928); Kromayer and Veith, Heerwesen und Kriegführung der Griechen und Römer (1928); Howard, ‘The Use and Abuse of Military History’ (1961 lecture; 1962)

strands.title: Chairs, journals and the soldier-scholar before 1960
strands.focus: In the British institutions examined here, university teaching developed alongside officer education. Oxford made military history a special subject after the South African War, created a lectureship in 1905 and a chair in 1909, whose first holder, Spenser Wilkinson, called military history ‘the effort to understand war’; the chair, vacant from 1939, went to Cyril Falls in 1946 rather than Liddell Hart. Trinity College, Cambridge, appointed Fortescue its first lecturer in military history in 1913. At King’s College London Frederick Maurice held a chair of military studies from 1927; the department closed in 1948. In the United States the American Military History Foundation was incorporated in 1933 after discussions among ‘military and civilian archival personnel’; its journal (1937) became Military Affairs in 1941 and nearly collapsed in 1957. Strachan (2002) calls Liddell Hart and Falls ‘in many ways more a journalist than an academic’ and writes that before Howard’s appointment almost nobody who studied the history of war had not experienced it.
strands.works: Wilkinson, The University and the Study of War (1909); Fortescue, Military History (1914), lecture I; Maurice, ‘On the Uses of the Study of War’ (1927), as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch; Society for Military History chronology (1933–69 entries)

strands.title: War, state and society before the ‘new military history’
strands.focus: Wilkinson’s inaugural lecture (1909) held that ‘as the State is, so will its army be’ and that in war ‘the architectonic art is policy or politics, not strategy or generalship’. Maurice (1927, as quoted by Morgan-Owen and Finch) counted statecraft, economics, raw materials, science, industry and civilian morale as of ‘prime importance’ to the study of war. Hancock, editing the civil official histories, treated the armed forces as ‘no more than the cutting edge of the nation at war’ (as quoted by the same authors). Roberts (1955) proposed tactical change with wider institutional effects. Quincy Wright’s foreword (1942) describes a study of war begun at the University of Chicago in 1926 that involved ‘over fifty studies by research assistants and members of the faculty’; only the foreword is read. Karsten (1984) calls such questions the ‘new’ military history while conceding that ‘some scholars explored such questions in the past’. Hintze, Vagts, Ritter and Ropp are not yet read for this entry.
strands.works: Wilkinson (1909); Maurice, inaugural lecture (1927); Wright, A Study of War (1942), foreword; Hancock and Gowing, British War Economy (1949); Roberts, ‘The Military Revolution, 1560–1660’ (1955 lecture); Karsten (1984), opening

strands.title: Ancient historians on testimony, terrain and experience
strands.focus: Thucydides tests eyewitness accounts against one another and says Spartan secrecy and bragging prevent accurate numbers at Mantinea. Polybius requires the study of documents, the survey of places and political experience, holds that no one without experience of war can write well about it, and judges Ephorus’ land battles by the ground; his polemic is also self-promotion. Arrian prefers Ptolemy and Aristobulus because they served on the campaign. Grundy (1911) calls Thucydides’ narrative ‘in the main a military history’ subordinated to political teaching, and Kromayer (1903) adopts and qualifies Polybius’ criticism of Ephorus. Delbrück (1913, p. 16) asks: ‘Ought we to believe what Caesar informs us of concerning the gigantic armies of the Gauls, whose conquest is his glory, since we have now seen that neither Napoleon nor Frederick in this respect is to be trusted?’; Caesar’s text itself was not read. Herodotus and Xenophon appear only through modern critics: Delbrück (1913) notes that Herodotus wrote ‘forty or fifty years after the events’, Grundy (1901) that in military matters he ‘seems to have possessed little, if any, special knowledge’, and Kromayer (1903, p. 93) finds Xenophon’s account of Mantinea one-sided. These writers are precursors of a genre, not a single origin of the field.
strands.works: Thucydides, History 1.22, 5.68; Polybius, Histories 12.25e–28a, 3.33, 3.48; Arrian, Anabasis, preface; Grundy (1901), preface, and (1911), pp. 7–9; Kromayer (1903), pp. 93–96; Delbrück, Numbers in History (1913), pp. 8–10, 16

events.label: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War (1.22, 5.68)
events.support: Placed only in the fifth century BCE: a contemporary narrator of the war who says he relied on what he saw and on tested reports (1.22) and recounts the battle of Mantinea, 418 BCE (5.68). The passages read do not date the composition, which may have continued after 401 BCE; ‘approximate’ marks that. A precursor of the genre, not the field’s beginning.

events.label: Polybius, Histories (12.25e–28a; 3.33, 3.48)

continuation.basis: The field is older and broader than these selected works; ancient precursors are not its beginning, and no researched universal interval is proposed.

chronology.interpretation: Use dated works with an explicit selective scope. Thucydides, Polybius and Arrian are context: precursors of the genre, placed only by century, not a lineage or the field’s first years. Oman, Fortescue, Delbrück, Grundy and Kromayer (1898–1903) are a selected cluster of modern scholarly work, not a foundation date; Kromayer’s 1900 expedition is context for his 1903 volume. Official and semi-official histories (Edmonds 1922, Morison 1947, Matloff and Snell 1953) and the American society and journal (1933, 1937) are selected later events, not the beginnings of official or American military history. Howard 1961 and Keegan 1976 are contributions to an older field, not its first and last years. Later memoir dates are evidence dates, not new personal interventions by Howard.
retain: Multiple paradigms, colonial/guerrilla limits of Keegan's frame, and collaboration/editorial labour.
Ancient precursors are not a continuous lineage; the modern selection concentrates on British, American and German scholarship.
unresolved: If phase bars are useful, define their subject and geography; do not construct a universal beginning from the oldest source in this selection.
Composition dates of the ancient works were not checked; they are placed by century only. Caesar, Herodotus and Xenophon are discussed only through modern critics and are not dated here.

political.label: Political history
political.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.

political.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

strands.title: The new political history of Britain, 1993–2011
strands.focus: After the Social History round on Stedman Jones (1992–93), British political history took the linguistic turn and argued with it. Vernon's Politics and the People (1993) held that between the Reform Acts 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed (p. 107, as quoted by Tilly); his Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered Epstein, Wahrman, Joyce, Antony Taylor and Anna Clark under 'new narratives'. Vernon credited Epstein's late-1980s articles, subsequently collected in Radical Expression (1994), as inspirational 'for those like myself who followed into the field' of 'the new cultural history of British politics' (2004). Lawrence and Taylor's Party, State and Society (1997) set out to 'examine critically "electoral sociology"' (as quoted by LoPatin), and Lawrence's Speaking for the People (1998) questioned 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party' for the politics of place and gender; Vernon found it 'ambitious, but ultimately flawed' (1999) and Lawrence answered, in a response posted in 2010, that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches must be combined. Electing Our Masters (2009) followed the hustings and the platform; in 2011 Lawrence argued for a 'conservative' rather than 'liberal' modernity. Positions within one field, not a school; the debate entry languages_of_class holds the exchanges.

women.label: Women’s history
women.date_label: Nineteenth-century and interwar work; renewed expansion from the 1960s
women.description: Studies women as historical actors and examines work, family, politics, and structures of power. Earlier scholarship, activism, teaching, and documentary collecting precede the field’s expansion alongside later feminist movements. Recovery, institutional growth, rediscovery, and methodological disagreement overlap; this is not a field created from nothing in the 1960s or one account of a shared female experience.

social.label: New social history
social.description: An overlapping field of work, class formation, households, community and collective action. Thompson, Davis and Gutman already integrate culture and agency; demographic and mobility studies use distinct evidence. Davidoff and Hall connect gender and middle-class life; Chakrabarty and Cooper investigate colonial labor and the limits of inherited categories. Scott’s critique makes experience itself a historical question, not something to discard.

Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm; Herbert Gutman, Work, Culture, and Society in Industrializing America (1976); Natalie Zemon Davis, Society and Culture in Early Modern France (1975); Charles Tilly; E. A. Wrigley and historical demography. Earlier social inquiry provides comparisons, not membership in a later school. Further readings: Davidoff and Hall, Family Fortunes (1987); Chakrabarty, Rethinking Working-Class History (1989); Scott, “The Evidence of Experience” (1991); Cooper, Decolonization and African Society (1996). Geoff Eley and Keith Nield: “Why does social history ignore politics?” (1980).

indigenous.scope_note: A selective grouping of independently rooted Indigenous historical practices and decolonizing research, with Andean, Haudenosaunee, Ojibwe, Cree, Métis, Wendat, Māori, Osage, Native Hawaiian, Yukon and Australian examples. Earlier writing, community knowledge, academic historical scholarship and decolonizing methodology have different histories. Community historians, academic historians and outside collaborators have different positions. Neither anthropology nor European theory is their common origin; no selection stands for every nation or protocol. Membership is a contextual intellectual contribution, not a binary Indigenous-identity classification. Journal counts are venue-based publication proxies and cannot date the origins of these practices or identify Indigenous authorship. Academic Indigenous history includes documented collaborations with scholars working across historical, anthropological and geographical inquiries. Shared research subjects do not establish intellectual descent. Later source dates are separate from earlier events; only Leddy’s 2010 article is accepted here as a selected post-2000 intervention.

strands.title: Land, identity and colonial change
strands.focus: Natick land loss, kinship and the making of an extinction narrative.
strands.works: Dispossession by Degrees (1997)

strands.title: Authority over research
strands.focus: Self-determination affects questions, methods and knowledge ownership; researcher positions differ within as well as across communities.
strands.works: Decolonizing Methodologies (1999)

strands.title: Māori scholarship and material culture
strands.focus: An earlier historical/anthropological trajectory, not a precursor stage superseded by one later method.
strands.works: Vikings of the Sunrise (1938); The Coming of the Maori (1949)

strands.title: Criticism of institutions and researchers
strands.focus: Deloria’s manifesto supplies a distinct Native American intervention; specific chapters remain to be read.
strands.works: Custer Died for Your Sins (1969)

strands.title: Tribal and family historians
strands.focus: Wilson connects historical interpretation to sustained relationships and authority to share particular knowledge.
strands.works: “American Indian History or Non-Indian Perceptions…” (1996)

strands.title: Collaborative Yukon life narratives
strands.focus: Three elders and an anthropologist collaborate; life interviewing and transmitted traditions remain distinct practices.
strands.works: Life Lived Like a Story (1990)

strands.title: Australian Indigenist methodology
strands.focus: Rigney’s 1999 article broadens the methodological bibliography; detailed arguments await primary reading.
strands.works: “Internationalization…” (1999)

strands.title: Aymara direction and Andean oral history
strands.focus: Rivera describes THOA’s collective work and community review; research priorities do not belong solely to outside intellectuals.
strands.works: “El potencial epistemológico…” (1987); THOA’s Santos Marka T’ula project (1984), discussed there

strands.title: Distinct voices in collaborative history
strands.focus: Rita and Jackie Huggins’s life-history collaboration and their coauthored place article with Jacobs retain different author positions. Heiss’s 1998 review foregrounds oral testimony and historical authority.
strands.works: Auntie Rita (1994); Kooramindanjie (1995); Heiss on Sister Girl (1998)

strands.title: Narratives, place and institutional interpretation
strands.focus: Cruikshank’s 1993 discussion contrasts community uses of tradition with institutional demands. Her account of Gitksan and Wet’suwet’en testimony questions treating performed histories only as containers of facts.
strands.works: Claiming Legitimacy (1993), selected sections

strands.title: Early Andean manuscript history
strands.focus: An early colonial-period historical manuscript, situated in a Christian and royal political framework. It demonstrates earlier Indigenous-authored historical writing without making a modern field or THOA descend directly from it.
strands.works: El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno (manuscript c. 1615/1616)

strands.title: Haudenosaunee histories in print
strands.focus: Cusick’s preface presents gathering materials and translation as historical work. The 1828 second edition is a verified witness; printed publication is not the origin of the traditions it recounts.
strands.works: Sketches of Ancient History of the Six Nations (checked second edition, 1828)

strands.title: Historical argument and colonial commemoration
strands.focus: Apess challenges colonial historical judgments and Pilgrim celebration. His Christian moral argument is an earlier intervention; no borrowing by later theorists is asserted.
strands.works: Eulogy on King Philip (1836), selected paragraphs

strands.title: Ojibwe oral knowledge and written history
strands.focus: Warren’s history draws on relatives and tribal leaders while addressing white readers. The publisher’s discussion retains the author’s nineteenth-century assumptions and limitations.
strands.works: History of the Ojibway People (first publication, 1885)

strands.title: Māori manuscript authorship and colonial publication
strands.focus: Te Rangikāheke’s genealogy and historical narration survive within manuscripts and Grey’s altered publications. Attribution reveals an Indigenous author behind texts circulated under a governor’s name.
strands.works: Historical and genealogical manuscripts before 1854; material reused in Grey’s publications, 1853–55

strands.title: Cree narration and interwar writing
strands.focus: Thunderchild’s narration, Ahenakew’s 1923 recording and literary writing, his 1929 publication, and the 1973 edited book carry different dates and authorial roles. Cuthand’s 1995 criticism makes editorial selection visible.
strands.works: 1923 narration/recording; Cree Trickster Tales (1929); Voices of the Plains Cree (1973; 1995 introduction)

strands.title: Tainui genealogies and historical writing
strands.focus: Jones’s Māori-language historical work and the history of its publication distinguish interwar research from the 1995 posthumous volume. The institutional biography describes disputed reuse of an earlier English manuscript.
strands.works: Māhinārangi (1929); English historical manuscript by c. 1936; Ngā iwi o Tainui (1995, posthumous)

strands.title: Canadian historical synthesis and regional inquiry
strands.focus: Dickason’s studies of representations and historical synthesis sit alongside Stonechild and Waiser’s Saskatchewan study. These are different scales and collaborations, not one doctrinal programme.
strands.works: The Myth of the Savage (1984); Canada’s First Nations (1992); Stonechild and Waiser, Loyal Till Death (1997)

strands.title: Métis scholarship and criticism of representation
strands.focus: Adams’s colonial and class interpretation and LaRocque’s criticism of representation broaden the 1970s bibliography. Her 1999 dissertation p. 34 explicitly connects the earlier book to curriculum research and resistance. These are distinct intellectual positions.
strands.works: Prison of Grass (1975); Defeathering the Indian (1975)

strands.title: Wendat autohistory and historical interpretation
strands.focus: Sioui’s author interview supplies an explicit historiographical proposal about self-interpretation and oral transmission. His moral account remains attributed and situated; French and English publication dates are distinct.
strands.works: Pour une autohistoire amérindienne (1989); author interview (1991); English translation by Sheila Fischman (1992)

strands.title: Historical synthesis and Native history institutions
strands.focus: McNickle’s 1949 work and role in creating the Newberry centre in 1972 establish an earlier bibliography and institutional contribution. Neither the centre nor a university is treated as the origin of Indigenous historical knowledge.
strands.works: They Came Here First: The Epic of the American Indian (1949); Newberry history centre (1972)

strands.title: Osage historical writing across the century
strands.focus: Mathews’s 1932 work and 1961 history supply earlier and mid-century examples. The publisher describes oral and documentary historical resources; detailed methodological claims await the works.
strands.works: Wah’Kon-Tah (1932); The Osages: Children of the Middle Waters (1961)

strands.title: Hawaiian land history and sovereignty
strands.focus: Kameʻeleihiwa’s land history and Trask’s political essays provide distinct Hawaiian contributions. Hawaiian-language historiography has earlier authors; neither regional programme is a subset of the Māori examples.
strands.works: Native Land and Foreign Desires (1992); From a Native Daughter (1993; revised 1999)

strands.title: Aboriginal interviews and life writing
strands.focus: Gilbert’s interviews and Ginibi’s autobiography broaden the historical bibliography beyond university monographs. Their forms and authorial positions differ from each other and from community-transmitted oral histories.
strands.works: Living Black (1977); Don’t Take Your Love to Town (1988)

strands.title: Aymara political and local history
strands.focus: Mamani’s catalogued 1991 study complements the existing collective-history strand. The period 1866–1935 belongs to the subject, not its publication or the foundation of THOA.
strands.works: Taraqu, 1866–1935 (published 1991)

strands.title: Stó:lō community–university historical practice
strands.focus: Community priorities, cultural teaching, archives and university instruction contribute different resources. Planning in 1997 preceded the first class in 1998; elders, hosts and students also participated.
strands.works: Field-school planning (1997); first class (1998); later accounts (2009, 2011, 2016)

strands.title: Indigenous labour and exchange
strands.focus: A labour-history inquiry into Indigenous economic participation; distinct from a methodological origin claim.
strands.works: After the Fur Trade (1992)

strands.title: Native–newcomer and institutional histories
strands.focus: Historical synthesis and residential-school inquiry connect policy, institutions and Indigenous experiences.
strands.works: Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989); Shingwauk’s Vision (1996)

strands.title: Middle-ground interpretation
strands.focus: Cultural interaction exceeds a simple assimilation/persistence account. Great Lakes circumstances do not supply a universal account of colonization.
strands.works: The Middle Ground (1991)

strands.title: Colonial geography and displacement
strands.focus: Historical geography examines the colonial transformation of British Columbia and its effects on land and society.
strands.works: The Resettlement of British Columbia (1997)

strands.title: Related settler-colonial scholarship
strands.focus: A related bibliography on settler colonialism and anthropology. Book arguments and transmission remain outside this metadata-level inclusion.
strands.works: Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology (1999)

strands.title: Community and academic relationships at Serpent River
strands.focus: Family knowledge, scholarly dialogue and mentorship shape historical practice; the roles remain distinct.
strands.works: Interviewing Nookomis and Other Reflections (2010)

philhistory.label: Explanation & objectivity debates
philhistory.date_label: Earlier roots · Becker address 1931 · Hempel 1942 · Carr 1961 · Elton 1967
philhistory.description: Disputes concern general laws, understanding actions, historical facts, and the possibility of objectivity. Analytic philosophy’s covering-law debate overlaps with historians’ arguments about evidence and interpretation without being identical to them. Narrative theory enters a discussion already under way.
philhistory.representative_figures_and_works: Becker’s 1931 address (published 1932); Hempel, “The Function of General Laws in History” (1942); Dray, Laws and Explanation in History (1957); Carr, What Is History? (1961); Elton, The Practice of History (1967).

representative_people.context: Connects everyday inquiry, social memory and changing interpretation while retaining critical checks.
representative_people.works: Everyman His Own Historian (address 1931; publication 1932)

representative_people.context: Proposes testable laws and initial conditions, allowing probability and incomplete explanation sketches.
representative_people.works: The Function of General Laws in History (1942)

representative_people.context: Challenges reducing all historical explanations to a covering-law model; rational action and pragmatic questions are distinct concerns.
representative_people.works: Laws and Explanation in History (1957)

representative_people.context: Treats selection, interpretation and research as reciprocal while rejecting equal validity for every account.
representative_people.works: What Is History? (1961)

representative_people.context: Addresses research, imagination, writing and teaching; Mink cites his insistence on immersion in a period.
representative_people.works: The Practice of History (1967)

representative_people.context: Historian of evidence who distinguishes origins from explanation and treats traces as answers to questions under evidential constraints.
representative_people.works: Apologie pour l’histoire ou Métier d’historien (1949)

representative_people.context: Earlier philosophical questions about history’s uses, the explanation of moral values and the conditions of objectivity. This is not membership in the later covering-law debate.
representative_people.works: On the Use and Abuse of History for Life (1874); On the Genealogy of Morals (1887), preface, II.12–13 and III.12

representative_people.context: A specific interlocutor in Nietzsche’s account of genealogical explanation: Nietzsche names his book as a stimulus and disputes its hypotheses. Included at this mediated scope, not as a founder of later historical philosophy.
representative_people.works: The Origin of the Moral Feelings (1877), as discussed in Nietzsche’s Genealogy preface §§4–7

representative_people.context: Nietzsche calls him a teacher while challenging the value assigned to pity. This explains one background to a critique of values, not agreement or an independent reading of Schopenhauer.
representative_people.works: Schopenhauer’s account of pity as discussed in Nietzsche, Genealogy preface §5 (1887)

representative_people.context: Combines rhetorical analysis of historiography with attention to source-based construction; adopts Barthes while questioning a uniform disappearance of concern with reality.
representative_people.works: “Analysing the discourse of history” (1983); The Inventions of History (1990)

representative_people.context: Examines how historical discourse constructs signification and claims reference. Historians’ engagement includes productive use and criticism, not one settled verdict on evidence.
representative_people.works: “The Discourse of History” (1967); “The Reality Effect” (1968)

representative_people.context: Michelet explicitly appropriates humanity’s self-making as a historical principle; original Vico is not read here.
representative_people.works: Scienza nuova as recalled in Michelet (1869)

representative_people.context: A named resource against fixed innate explanations in Michelet’s account of historical formation.
representative_people.works: Passage quoted by Michelet (1869), p. 142

representative_people.context: Lamprecht credits a conception of collective historical life; this is a mediated resource, not a universal origin claim.
representative_people.works: Ideas concerning the History of Mankind, as cited by Lamprecht (1905)

representative_people.context: Reflects on the reciprocal formation of historian and history through research and historical imagination.
representative_people.works: Preface to History of France (1869), pp. 143–144

representative_people.context: Asks how source survival and artistic forms shape historical perception.
representative_people.works: The Waning of the Middle Ages (1924), preface and chapter XIX opening

representative_people.context: Combines close documentary work with relations among events, peoples and epochs. Historical individuality and religious commitments coexist; his selected European scope and civilizational judgments are contestable, and he is not the sole origin of criticism.
representative_people.works: History of the Popes (1834–1836; Austin translation 1840); 1824 historical preface; lectures on epochs (1854); selected World History reflections

representative_people.context: Source search, criticism and interpretation cooperate. Material remains, accounts and monuments are not interchangeable; neither authentic documents nor individual intentions alone yield a complete historical explanation.
representative_people.works: Grundriss der Historik (public edition 1867; consulted Andrews English 1893), §§1–11, 20–24, 28–41

representative_people.context: Develops a foundation for human sciences encompassing history, theory and practical judgments. Later attention to expression and shared historical worlds qualifies an account based only on individual psychology; the later primary text remains separately scoped.
representative_people.works: Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883), chapters 1, 2, 6; The Formation of the Historical World in the Human Sciences (1910), through editors’ introduction and SEP

representative_people.context: Historical thought responds to present questions while drawing on preserved documents. His distinction between living history and chronicle is idealist, not a distinction between important and trivial subjects or an instruction to disregard evidence.
representative_people.works: Theory and History of Historiography (Italian 1917; consulted 1921 Ainslie translation from 1919 edition), I.1

representative_people.context: Re-enactment reconstructs an intelligible act of thought through evidence, not its original sensations or total immediacy. Skinner later credits changing questions and question/answer logic while emphasizing other philosophical resources.
representative_people.works: An Autobiography (1939), reception through Skinner; The Idea of History (1946, posthumous), Epilegomena §4, selected paragraphs

representative_people.context: Dilthey expands the critical project toward historical reason and embodied human experience. This identifies a named philosophical resource, not agreement with every Kantian premise.
representative_people.works: Critique of Pure Reason; Dilthey’s Introduction to the Human Sciences (1883) as a documented reworking

representative_people.context: Dilthey contests speculative system-building while adapting objective spirit to shared historical forms. A productive appropriation with disagreement; the original Hegel corpus is not independently collated here.
representative_people.works: Objective spirit; Dilthey’s Die Jugendgeschichte Hegels (1906) and later Formation project as documented reception

representative_people.context: Hermeneutics and religious life become objects of Dilthey’s editorial, biographical and philosophical work; the intellectual setting extends beyond a private psychological portrait.
representative_people.works: Hermeneutical writings and letters; Dilthey’s 1860 hermeneutical study and Leben Schleiermachers, volume I (1870) as reception

representative_people.context: Language use and rule-following supply questions about intelligible action. This selection identifies a conceptual resource; particular historical reception is documented separately through Skinner and Geertz.
representative_people.works: Philosophical Investigations (1953), selected §§19, 23, 43, 65–67, 198–202, 241–242

representative_people.context: Distinguishes conceptual errors, competent performances and what an act accomplishes. This is a resource for discussing explanations of action, not proof that every historical philosopher borrowed from him.
representative_people.works: The Concept of Mind (1949), I and II.1–3; The Thinking of Thoughts (1968)

strands.title: Genealogy, values and historical explanation
strands.focus: Nietzsche’s critique asks both how moral judgments arise and what they are worth; Rée and Schopenhauer are distinct interlocutors. Origin and later function must not be conflated.
strands.works: Genealogy (1887), preface and II.12–13

strands.title: Rhetoric, reference and historical achievement
strands.focus: Barthes analyzes the presentation of reality; Bann uses that analysis while questioning its scope and preserving source-based scrutiny. Formal analysis alone does not decide a historical claim’s truth.
strands.works: History/reality essays (1967–1968); Bann (1983/1990)

strands.title: The historian, surviving sources and the historical picture
strands.focus: Michelet’s account of reciprocal formation and Huizinga’s warning about surviving art raise different questions about historical knowledge; they do not deny the need for evidence.
strands.works: Michelet (1869); Huizinga (1924)

strands.title: Evidence, understanding and the historical question
strands.focus: Droysen, Dilthey, Croce and Collingwood offer different accounts of what inquiry does with traces, thought, context and practical concerns. These are explicit conceptual resources, not a common doctrine or a proved genealogy of later debate.
strands.works: Selected methodological texts (1867–1946)

strands.title: Language use and following rules
strands.focus: Wittgenstein examines varied activities and similarities rather than one essence of language. Following a rule involves a practice; an interpretation cannot supply its own application without limit.
strands.works: Philosophical Investigations, selected §§19–242

strands.title: Knowing how, action and accomplishment
strands.focus: Ryle distinguishes competent action from both an automatic movement and a performance governed by an endless series of prior theoretical decisions. A richer action description identifies purpose and circumstances.
strands.works: The Concept of Mind, II.1–3; The Thinking of Thoughts

strands.title: Narrative and historical understanding
strands.focus: White identifies particular philosophical interlocutors rather than responding to one undifferentiated philosophy of history.
strands.works: Metahistory (1973),2–3 notes

strands.title: Laws, probability and explanation sketches
strands.focus: Hempel’s demand for testable relations permits incomplete research proposals and probabilistic accounts.
strands.works: General Laws (1942)

strands.title: Action and the limits of one explanatory model
strands.focus: Dray’s challenge includes reasons, uniqueness and pragmatic questions; it is not a ban on all generalization.
strands.works: Laws and Explanation (1957); Nature of Historical Explanation (1952)

strands.title: Selection, relevance and revisable interpretation
strands.focus: Becker and Carr preserve evidence while disputing self-interpreting facts; they do not offer identical positions.
strands.works: Everyman (1931/1932); What Is History? (1961),chapter1

strands.title: Historical craft, imagination and instruction

strands.works: Practice of History (1967); Skinner1997opening extract

strands.focus: Walsh’s scope distinguishes questions about inquiry from philosophies of the whole historical process.
strands.works: Introduction (1951)

newleft.label: New Left & radical history (US)
newleft.description: Challenges consensus interpretations through studies of class, race, capitalism, and empire. Radical diplomatic, labour, and slavery histories overlap with new social history but differ in politics and method. Their engagements with Black history do not supply that field’s independent origins. Gutman’s cultural labor history also criticizes some New Left institutional accounts. Alice and Staughton Lynd make organizer testimony and participant review part of research practice; Zinn’s selective Marxian commitments differ from Genovese’s paternalism interpretation.
newleft.representative_figures_and_works: William Appleman Williams, The Tragedy of American Diplomacy (1959)—a different writer from Eric Williams; Staughton Lynd; Eugene Genovese, Roll, Jordan, Roll (1974); Herbert Gutman, Work, Culture, and Society (1976); Radical History Review (1973).

representative_people.context: Interprets slavery through class, culture and paternalism as contested domination. His preface’s national-culture framing and later criticism remain visible; paternalism is not a claim of benign slavery.

representative_people.context: Studies work discipline and differentiated working-class cultures; explicitly adapts British methods and criticizes some New Left labor history. His 1973 article excludes nonwhite and bound workers from its detailed scope.

racial_formation.label: Racial formation
racial_formation.description: Investigates how racial categories and meanings are produced and contested through social, political and economic relations. Omi and Winant’s programme treats race as historically specific and consequential, not as a biological essence or a simple expression of another social category.
racial_formation.scope_note: A distinct theoretical programme relevant to histories of racialization, not a synonym for Black history or all scholarship about race. Original 1986 and revised 1994 editions remain distinct. The checked course extract is labelled second edition; its retyped pagination and edition attribution have not been independently authenticated. Intersectional analysis connects racial inquiry with gender, class and sexuality without being identical to racial-formation theory.
